questions.question_text: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with reward, motivation, and movement?
questions.option_b: dopamine
questions.explanation: Dopamine underlies reward and motor control; its loss is implicated in Parkinson's, its excess in some schizophrenia symptoms. Serotonin links to mood; GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter; acetylcholine to muscle action and memory.

questions.question_text: The sympathetic nervous system is responsible for:
questions.option_b: the fight-or-flight response — arousing the body for action
questions.explanation: The sympathetic branch mobilizes the body under stress (raising heart rate, dilating pupils). The PARASYMPATHETIC branch handles rest-and-digest — the two are opposing halves of the autonomic system.

questions.question_text: A researcher uses an fMRI primarily to:
questions.option_a: measure electrical activity at the scalp
questions.option_b: image brain structure and activity by tracking blood-oxygen flow
questions.explanation: fMRI tracks blood flow to show which regions are active during tasks, giving both structure and function. EEG measures scalp electrical activity (good time resolution, poor spatial) — a common contrast.

questions.question_text: Damage to the amygdala would most likely impair:
questions.option_b: fear processing and emotional responses
questions.explanation: The amygdala is central to fear and emotional salience. Coordination is the cerebellum; new explicit memories the hippocampus; language Broca's/Wernicke's areas — match structure to function.

questions.question_text: Chunking improves memory by:
questions.option_a: increasing the number of separate items to recall
questions.option_b: grouping items into meaningful units to expand working-memory capacity
questions.explanation: Grouping (e.g., a phone number as three chunks) lets limited working memory hold more by treating clusters as single units. It expands effective capacity beyond the ~7±2 individual items.

questions.question_text: The misinformation effect, studied by Loftus, shows that:
questions.option_b: exposure to misleading information after an event can distort eyewitness memory
questions.explanation: Post-event suggestions can reshape what people 'remember' — undermining eyewitness reliability. Memory is reconstructive, not a faithful recording, which is the deeper point.

questions.question_text: Solving a problem suddenly with an 'aha!' moment, rather than step by step, illustrates:
questions.option_b: insight
questions.explanation: Insight is the sudden realization of a solution. Algorithms are step-by-step guarantees; heuristics are mental shortcuts. The contrast is between deliberate strategies and sudden restructuring.

questions.question_text: The framing effect demonstrates that:
questions.option_a: wording has no impact on decisions
questions.option_b: the way options are presented (e.g., '90% survival' vs '10% mortality') alters choices
questions.explanation: Identical information framed differently shifts preferences — proof that decisions aren't purely rational. '90% survival' feels better than '10% mortality' despite being equivalent.

questions.question_text: Observing and imitating a model, as in Bandura's Bobo doll study, illustrates:
questions.option_b: observational (social) learning
questions.explanation: Children who watched aggressive models imitated them — learning by observation without direct reinforcement. This challenged the view that all learning requires personal reward or punishment.

questions.question_text: According to Erikson, the central crisis of adolescence is:
questions.option_b: identity vs role confusion
questions.explanation: Adolescents work to form a coherent self — identity vs role confusion. Trust vs mistrust is infancy; integrity vs despair is late adulthood. Each Eriksonian stage pairs with a life period.

questions.question_text: Harlow's monkey experiments with wire and cloth 'mothers' demonstrated that:
questions.option_b: contact comfort is more important than nourishment for attachment
questions.explanation: Infant monkeys clung to the soft cloth mother even when the wire one provided food — showing attachment rests on comfort, not just feeding. This overturned the 'cupboard theory' of love.

questions.question_text: A token economy applies which principle to shape behavior?
questions.option_b: operant conditioning through secondary reinforcers
questions.explanation: Tokens are secondary reinforcers exchangeable for rewards, reinforcing desired behavior operantly. It's a direct application of reinforcement, not the stimulus-pairing of classical conditioning.

questions.question_text: The bystander effect predicts that a victim is LESS likely to get help when:
questions.option_b: many bystanders are present, diffusing responsibility
questions.explanation: More witnesses → diffusion of responsibility → each person assumes someone else will act. Counterintuitively, a lone bystander is MORE likely to help than one in a crowd.

questions.question_text: In Festinger's theory, cognitive dissonance is the discomfort arising from:
questions.option_b: a conflict between beliefs and actions, motivating attitude change
questions.explanation: Holding inconsistent cognitions (e.g., 'smoking is bad' yet smoking) creates tension people resolve by changing attitudes or behavior. The drive to reduce dissonance often shifts attitudes to match actions.

questions.question_text: Freud's defense mechanism of projection involves:
questions.option_b: attributing one's own unacceptable impulses to others
questions.option_c: redirecting impulses to a safer target
questions.explanation: Projection assigns your own unwanted feelings to someone else ('You're the one who's angry!'). Regression is reverting; displacement is redirecting; denial is refusing reality — distinguish the mechanisms.

questions.question_text: Conformity in Asch's line-judgment study was driven mainly by:
questions.option_b: normative social influence — the desire to fit in with the group
questions.explanation: Participants gave obviously wrong answers to match the group — normative influence (fitting in), not because they couldn't see the lines. Milgram's studies, by contrast, tap obedience to authority.

questions.question_text: A persistent, irrational fear of a specific object or situation that disrupts life is a:
questions.option_b: specific phobia
questions.explanation: A phobia is an intense, focused fear (heights, spiders) out of proportion to actual danger. Generalized anxiety is diffuse and free-floating, not tied to one trigger.

questions.question_text: The biopsychosocial model explains disorders as arising from:
questions.option_b: the interaction of biological, psychological, and social factors
questions.explanation: Modern psychology rejects single-cause explanations: genes, thoughts, and environment jointly shape disorders. This integrated view replaced older models that isolated one cause.

questions.question_text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) treat depression by:
questions.option_b: increasing serotonin availability in the synapse
questions.explanation: SSRIs block serotonin reuptake, leaving more in the synapse to improve mood over weeks. The name is the mechanism: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor.

questions.question_text: The diathesis-stress model proposes that psychological disorders result from:
questions.option_b: a predisposition (diathesis) activated by environmental stress
questions.explanation: A latent vulnerability (genetic or biological) only manifests as a disorder when triggered by sufficient stress. Neither factor alone is enough — it's the interaction, echoing the biopsychosocial view.
